title: The tangent-two-theta theorem
subtitle: Independent reading companion to G3 023000
adaptation: Edited G3 lecture prose restructured into readable slide units; formulas and selected SVG geometric models are authored companion material.

slides.title: The central problem
slides.lead: The sine-two-theta theorem controls an operator that vanishes both at zero angle and at ninety degrees.
body: To recover a stronger geometric conclusion, we need to know which branch of that function we occupy. For a self-adjoint operator with an ordered two-block gap, an off-diagonal perturbation gives us exactly that information. The selected upper spectral subspace remains at angles strictly less than forty-five degrees from the original upper subspace. On that branch, the tangent of twice the angle is finite and can be controlled sharply. We will prove the result first in a two-by-two matrix, then explain a finite-dimensional graph proof that contains the central estimate.

slides.title: State the strong hypotheses
slides.lead: Let T be self-adjoint on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space H.
body: Let U reduce T. Assume the quadratic form of T on U is at least b times squared length, and its form on U perpendicular is at most a times squared length, with b greater than a. Write delta for b minus a. Perturb T by a self-adjoint operator H zero whose diagonal compressions onto U and onto U perpendicular both vanish. Denote the new operator by S. Let V be the upper reducing subspace selected from S.
slides.formula: off-diagonal perturbation and the selected upper branch

slides.title: State the strong hypotheses · further detail
slides.lead: To make the theorem precise, assume the quadratic form of S on V is at least b, and on V perpendicular at most a.
body: The source states the theorem with these matched bounds; when V is chosen from spectral subspaces, a separate spectral-repulsion result provides them. Suppose H zero has operator norm at most epsilon.

slides.title: State the strong hypotheses · continued
slides.lead: Then the maximal angle theta between U and V is strictly less than forty-five degrees, and delta times tangent of twice theta is at most twice epsilon.
body: This is an operator-norm theorem under the stated finite-dimensional hypotheses. We should not automatically promote it to every symmetric ideal norm without using a separately proved result.

slides.title: Derive the exact planar formula
slides.lead: Take T diagonal with entries b and a, where b is greater than a.
body: Let the perturbation H zero have zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries h. Then S has rows b, h and h, a. Consider an eigenvector for the upper eigenvalue, making an angle theta from the first coordinate axis. To diagonalize S, use an ordinary plane rotation. The off-diagonal entry in the rotated matrix is h times cosine twice theta minus half of b minus a times sine twice theta, with the sign depending on the orientation of the rotation. Setting that entry equal to zero gives tangent twice theta equal to two h divided by delta, with an appropriate choice of oriented theta. The acute absolute-angle version replaces h by its absolute value.

slides.title: Derive the exact planar formula · continued
slides.lead: Because arctangent of a finite nonnegative number lies below ninety degrees, theta equals half of that arctangent and is strictly below forty-five degrees.
body: The perturbation norm is the absolute value of h. Therefore delta times tangent twice theta equals twice the perturbation norm. The factor two is exactly sharp in this model. Unlike the sine-two-theta estimate, which approached equality only as h tended to zero, the tangent-two-theta estimate attains equality for every positive h in this planar family.

slides.title: How do we know the upper space stays on the correct branch?
slides.lead: We need a reason that does not depend on diagonalizing a two-by-two matrix.
body: Let P be projection onto U and let J equal twice P minus the identity. Center T at the midpoint c of a and b. The form-gap hypothesis gives a coercive inequality: the real part of the inner product of J times T minus c with x is at least half delta times the squared norm of x. Because the perturbation is off-diagonal, J H zero is skew-adjoint. Its quadratic form has zero real part. So the same coercive lower bound holds with S in place of T.

slides.title: How do we know the upper space stays on the correct branch? · further detail
slides.lead: This bound first proves spectral repulsion: no eigenvector of S can have an eigenvalue in the open gap.
body: Replacing the center c by any point between a and b gives the required contradiction. In finite dimensions, the gap contains no spectrum.

slides.title: How do we know the upper space stays on the correct branch? · continued
slides.lead: To select a subspace, choose V from the upper spectrum of S and let K be S minus c restricted to V.
body: K is positive and bounded below by half delta. Take any nonzero x in V, and evolve it by the decaying semigroup generated by K. Call the evolving vector y of time t. It stays in V and tends to zero as time grows. Consider its reflected quadratic form: the real inner product of J y with y. Its time derivative is negative twice the real inner product of J K y with y. By our coercive inequality, this derivative is at most negative delta times the squared norm of y. Integrate from time zero to infinity. The final reflected quadratic form vanishes.

slides.title: How do we know the upper space stays on the correct branch? · continued
slides.lead: Hence the initial value is at least delta times the integral of the squared norm of y, which is strictly positive for nonzero x.
body: But the reflected quadratic form of x is exactly the squared norm of its U component minus the squared norm of its perpendicular component. Therefore every nonzero vector of V has a strictly larger U component than perpendicular component. In finite dimensions this uniform positivity means the largest principal angle between V and U is below forty-five degrees. It also makes V a graph over U when the dimensions match, as they do for the selected upper spectral branch.

slides.title: Derive the sharp graph inequality
slides.lead: Represent V as the graph of an operator Z from U into U perpendicular.
body: The strict branch conclusion gives operator norm Z less than one. Its singular values are tangents of the principal angles. Relative to U plus U perpendicular, write T as diagonal blocks A plus and A minus. Write the off-diagonal perturbation using K and K adjoint. Thus S has upper-right block K adjoint and lower-left block K. A graph vector has components u and Z u. The condition that its image under S remains on the graph yields a Riccati equation. In words: K plus A minus Z equals Z A plus plus Z K adjoint Z. This equation contains both linear Sylvester terms and a quadratic correction from the off-diagonal coupling.

slides.title: Derive the sharp graph inequality · continued
slides.lead: Take a unit right singular vector u of Z associated with the largest singular value t.
body: Let v be its corresponding unit left singular vector. Then Z u equals t v and Z adjoint v equals t u. Pair the Riccati equation applied to u with v and take real parts. The diagonal terms contribute t times the difference between a Rayleigh quotient of A plus and a Rayleigh quotient of A minus. That difference is at least delta. The two off-diagonal terms combine into one minus t squared times the real part of the scalar pairing of v with K u. Therefore delta times t is at most epsilon times one minus t squared. The sign is legitimate because the branch proof already established t less than one. Rearrange and multiply by two.

slides.title: Derive the sharp graph inequality · continued
slides.lead: The scalar identity tangent twice theta equals twice tangent theta divided by one minus tangent squared theta now yields delta times tangent twice theta is at most twice epsilon, where theta is the largest principal angle.
body: This completes the finite-dimensional operator-norm argument. An equivalent route works with a maximal eigenvector in the permitted angular sector and controls the projection difference directly, avoiding a choice of graph coordinates.

slides.title: Interpret the cosine denominator
slides.lead: The difference between the doubled sine and doubled tangent is the denominator cosine twice theta.
body: For angles below forty-five degrees, cosine twice theta is positive. We can therefore pass from a bound on sine twice theta to a bound on tangent twice theta only if we can control that denominator. The off-diagonal spectral structure supplies the required positivity, and the graph argument obtains the sharp quantitative comparison. At forty-five degrees the denominator vanishes. The theorem says that no finite off-diagonal perturbation satisfying its hypotheses reaches that angle. A family can approach it as the coupling grows, but never attain it at finite size. This is a structural statement about a selected spectral branch. It is not true for an arbitrary reducing subspace chosen without regard to which side of the gap it occupies.

slides.title: Compare the two double-angle theorems
slides.lead: The sine-two-theta theorem needs a two-block gap for T and reducing subspaces for T and S.
body: It allows a general self-adjoint perturbation and gives delta times a doubled-sine norm at most twice the perturbation norm. The tangent-two-theta theorem adds off-diagonality, matching upper and lower spectral bounds for the selected perturbed subspace, and an operator-norm control. It gives both an angle strictly below forty-five degrees and the sharp doubled-tangent inequality. The stronger conclusion costs stronger hypotheses. It cannot be obtained simply by dividing the sine estimate by cosine twice theta without proving the branch and controlling that cosine.

slides.title: A final numerical check
slides.lead: Let delta equal two and let the coupling h equal one.
body: The formula gives tangent twice theta equal one, so theta is twenty-two point five degrees. Then cosine twice theta and sine twice theta both equal the square root of two divided by two. The sine-two-theta estimate gives two times approximately zero point seven zero seven at most two. The tangent-two-theta estimate gives two times one at most two, with equality. As h increases to ten, tangent twice theta equals ten and theta approaches forty-five degrees from below. The doubled sine becomes close to one, while the doubled tangent records the increasing difficulty of maintaining a graph with slope below one. The sharp doubled-tangent estimate is therefore a joint statement about a perturbation and the correctly selected spectral subspace. The spectral branch proof establishes that the cosine of twice every relevant angle is positive; the Riccati estimate then controls its reciprocal effect quantitatively.
slides.takeaway: The tangent-two-theta estimate combines off-diagonal symmetry with explicit spectral-branch control.
